look_here_first: Cool-season INTRODUCED annual; slender drooping and kinked panicle branches with groups of several relatively small (about 10–15 mm) multi-flowered awned spikelets. Lower sheaths often soft-haired. Do not identify it by awns alone.

best_field_traits: Annual cool-season bunch grass; senesces after seed set.
Panicle often open or nodding with thin flexuous branches, sometimes conspicuously kinked.
Spikelets often ~10–15 mm (excluding awns), usually containing several (about 6–11) florets.
Lemma awns frequently longer than on woodland brome, sometimes ~15 mm; lengths overlap other annual bromes.
Soft retrorse hairs on lower sheaths and often bent lower culms.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Clump including actual rooted annual base and fuzzy lower sheath
Whole nodding panicle with branching points in focus
One intact mature spikelet with millimeter scale showing number of florets
Separate fertile lemma and awn with 10× view
True membranous ligule at stem leaf collar
crew_field_check: LOOK AT THE SPIKELET, NOT JUST THE DROOP: all four bromes have several florets stacked along one spikelet, often with lemma awns. First decide ANNUAL vs PERENNIAL, then count florets, measure the entire spikelet, individual lemma and awn, and inspect the glume veins and leaf sheath hairs. Nodding inflorescences or long awns alone are not a species ID.
Measure actual mature spikelet(s) with a millimeter ruler.
Inspect lemma/glume or true ligule ONLY where detailed pixels or a collected macro are actually available.
Record uncertain grass to genus, don't force the species from one photo.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Compared to B. lanceolatus, usually shorter spikelets with fewer florets and more relaxed/kinked drooping branches; lanceolatus often has ~25–50 mm spikelets with 8–20 florets. Compared to native B. texensis, note Texas brome generally shorter 6–10 mm awns and requires lemma/branch dissection, not habitat alone. Unlike perennial B. pubescens, this is an annual and usually shorter-lived.

visual_comparison.memory_rule: Annual japonicus / lanceolatus / texensis versus perennial woodland pubescens. Small loose kinked heads japonicus; giant lance-shaped spikelets lanceolatus; damp shaded perennial pubescens; Texas annual texensis demands short-awn/lemma comparison.
